summary: TRILL normally lets one Appointed Forwarder per VLAN connect to non-TRILL networks, an active-standby model. This standards-track RFC defines Coordinated Multicast Trees to support active-active load sharing for high-performance applications. It updates RFC 6325.

eli5.summary: Instead of one guard working while another waits, both guards work at once and share the load, with a plan so they do not step on each other.

questions: what is trill coordinated multicast trees
what is a virtual rbridge in trill
how does trill active-active multicast work
subtitle: How TRILL edge switches stand in for one virtual RBridge and each claim their own multicast trees, so active-active edges pass the RPF check.

tldr.problem: TRILL's Appointed Forwarder gives only active-standby service to non-TRILL networks. Representing an active-active edge as one virtual RBridge breaks the multi-destination RPF check, because the normal tree calculation may leave an edge RBridge with no tree on which the virtual RBridge is a leaf.
tldr.mechanism: Each edge RBridge advertises an Affinity sub-TLV naming the virtual RBridge's nickname as its child on specific distribution trees. Every RBridge builds trees and RPF checks from those advertisements, and the edge RBridges split the trees among themselves.
tldr.outcome: Each member of the group ingresses and egresses multi-destination traffic only on its assigned trees, and CMT needs only a software upgrade. It updates RFC 6325 when Affinity sub-TLVs are present.

facts.label: Affinity capability bit
facts.value: bit 0 in TRILL-VER Sub-TLV Capability Flags

today: RFC 7783 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2016 that updates RFC 6325 when Affinity sub-TLVs are present. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Active-Active Needs New Trees
sections.content:
TRILL uses IS-IS as its control plane and a TRILL Header with a Hop Count. For end stations and bridged networks, RFC 6439 gives an active-standby model: for each VLAN only one RBridge on the link, the Appointed Forwarder (AF), is active. When the AF changes, remote forwarding tables may keep pointing at the old AF and traffic can be discarded at the egress.

High-performance applications want an active-active model. Customer devices are multi-homed to several RBridges and treat the uplinks independently using a Local Active-Active Link Protocol (LAALP) such as an MC-LAG bundle. An LAALP does not forward packets received on one member port to another member port of the same bundle, and the RBridges cannot exchange Hellos through it, so the AF method does not fit.

The proposal is to represent the edge group by a single virtual RBridge with its own campus-unique nickname. That causes a new problem. The tree and RPF (Reverse Path Forwarding) check algorithms in RFC 6325, as updated by RFC 7780, depend strictly on link cost and parent priority. Depending on the topology, an edge RBridge acting for the virtual RBridge may have no tree on which the virtual RBridge is a leaf, so it has no tree it can use.
sections.eli5: Two guards used to take turns, with one resting. Now both want to work at once, but the old rulebook has no street for the second guard to stand on.

sections.title: Scope and the Affinity Sub-TLV
sections.content:
This RFC lets an RBridge say which distribution trees a real or virtual child should hang from. It does this with the Affinity sub-TLV, which appears in Router Capability TLVs or MT Capability TLVs inside Link State PDUs. The code point and data structure are specified in RFC 7176, not here.

The specific methods apply where a virtual RBridge represents several RBridges connected to a customer device through an LAALP, or something similar, where the RBridges cannot see each other's Hellos. Other parts of an active-active solution, such as MC-LAG methods, are out of scope. See for example RFC 7781. The examples are for illustration only. Other applications may reuse the tree-association framework to attach to trees through a preferred path.

The scheme needs multiple multi-destination trees in the campus and every RBridge to support the Affinity sub-TLV. If either is missing, RBridges MUST support a fallback. The RFC gives guidelines but no mandatory fallback set.
sections.eli5: A small note, the Affinity note, lets a switch say "put this helper under my branch of the tree." The note format is defined in another RFC.

sections.title: Building Trees with Affinity
sections.content:
This RFC updates Section 4.5.1 of RFC 6325. Each RBridge that wants to be the parent of a child RBridge in a tree announces that with an Affinity sub-TLV naming the child by nickname. If an RBridge advertises one of its own nicknames as its child on a tree, that nickname is ignored when building other trees. The RPF check then enforces that only that RBridge may use the nickname for ingress or egress on that tree. Unicast least-cost paths are not affected.

When such a sub-TLV is present it MUST be used in building the tree, except when it conflicts with another one. If it is absent, or if any RBridge in the campus does not support it, trees are calculated as in RFC 6325 as updated by RFC 7780.

Each edge RBridge announces the virtual RBridge's nickname (RBv) in a Nickname sub-TLV (6) next to its own nicknames. Others can tell RBv is virtual because every RBridge that seems to hold it also asks for it as a child in one or more trees. Virtual RBridges are ignored when choosing tree roots. RBridges outside the group assume that multi-destination packets with Ingress Nickname RBv might use any tree that any group member advertises.

An RBridge shows support by announcing the TRILL Version sub-TLV and setting the Affinity capability bit.
sections.eli5: Each guard tells everyone which streets they cover for the shared helper. Everyone then draws their maps the same way, and only that guard is allowed on that street.

sections.title: Assigning Trees and Resolving Conflicts
sections.content:
Suppose there are n distribution trees and k edge RBridges in the group. The edge RBridges are sorted by IS-IS System ID and numbered from 0. Tree number ((tree_number) % k) + 1 is assigned to edge RBridge i, for tree numbers 1 to n. If n < k, the trees go to RB1 to RBn, and the rest, RBn+1 to RBk, do not take part in active-active forwarding for RBv.

Every group member advertises an Affinity sub-TLV with RBv as its child. For example, RB1 holding trees t1 and tk+1 advertises {RBv, Num of Trees = 2, t1, tk+1}.

Some records conflict and are handled as follows.

  • A record asking for RBroot as a child on a tree rooted at RBroot conflicts with root selection and MUST be ignored.
  • A record asking for nickname RBn as a child, when the advertiser is neither adjacent to RBn nor the owner of RBn, conflicts with the topology and MUST be ignored.
  • If different RBridges claim the same virtual RBridge on the same tree, the one holding the nickname with the highest priority to be a tree root (System ID as tiebreaker) keeps it. The others MUST stop advertising the conflicting records, recompute and advertise non-conflicting ones. Remote RBridges MUST honor the winner and ignore the others.
sections.eli5: The guards line up by number and take streets in turn. If two guards claim the same street, the one with the higher rank keeps it and the other picks again.

sections.title: Forwarding and Failure Handling
sections.content:
For multi-destination frames from a CE node, an edge RBridge RBk that has at least one tree with affinity for RBv does three things: it floods to locally attached CE nodes (with VLAN and multicast pruning), ingresses the frame with RBv as Ingress Nickname, and forwards it on one of the trees associated with RBk.

If RBk has no tree (probably because n is less than k), it MUST fall back to one of two options: stop forwarding CE frames and mark its CE ports disabled, so the CE nodes use only the assigned RBridges; or tunnel the frames to an RBridge that has an assigned tree. The tunnel mechanism is out of scope.

On egress, a multi-destination frame arriving at RBk on a tree for which it announced affinity for RBv MUST be forwarded to the CE members of RBv in the frame's VLAN. A frame arriving on any other tree MUST NOT be forwarded to those CE members. Forwarding to everything else follows RFC 6325.

The failure procedure is only a guideline. Members notice a failed member through IS-IS LSPs. They start a recovery timer T_rec, and if the member has not recovered when it expires, they redo the assignment and re-advertise. A starting RBridge starts timer T_i and the others start T_j. Each recalculates when its timer expires. Calculating at the wrong time can duplicate or lose packets, and duplication is described as more serious than loss. It is RECOMMENDED that T_j be less than T_i, with a reasonable default of 1/2 of T_i.
sections.eli5: A guard only lets traffic through on the streets they own and ignores the rest. When a guard goes missing the others wait a short time, in case the guard comes back, before dividing up the streets again.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support backward compatibility modes to work with RBridges that predate the Affinity sub-TLV. These MAY include tunneling and active-standby operation. Tunneling needs silicon changes, whereas CMT itself is a software upgrade.

As an example, a member would first stop using the virtual RBridge nickname for traffic from CE nodes, then stop active-active forwarding and fall back to active-standby based on local policy. Defining those policies is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If some switches are too old to understand the new notes, the guards go back to taking turns.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
RBridges in a campus are generally trusted routers. The authenticity of their LSPs and link-local PDUs can be enforced with regular IS-IS security mechanisms, including RFC 5310, and that covers the PDUs that carry Affinity sub-TLVs. Security issues specific to each application of the sub-TLV are left to the documents that define those applications. General TRILL security is in RFC 6325.

For IANA, this document is the reference for registering "Affinity sub-TLV support" (bit 0) in the "TRILL-VER Sub-TLV Capability Flags" registry. It also mentions the "AFFINITY" value 17 in the "Sub-TLVs for TLV 144" registry, but intentionally is not listed as a reference there; that remains RFC 7176.
sections.eli5: The switches are expected to be trustworthy, and passwords between them keep fakes out.

items.title: Ingress
items.text: Flood to local CE nodes, encapsulate with Ingress Nickname RBv, send on an assigned tree.

items.title: Egress, assigned tree
items.text: MUST forward to the CE members of RBv in the frame's VLAN.

items.title: Egress, other tree
items.text: MUST NOT forward to the CE members of RBv.

items.title: No tree (n < k)
items.text: Disable CE ports, or tunnel to an RBridge that has a tree.
